message: Built Texel-style automated tuning pipeline: self-play data generation (7 parallel shards, 4283 positions) + coordinate-descent optimizer
Ran Texel tuning against 4283 self-play positions; overrode 2 parameters that contradicted basic chess principles (isolated-pawn bonus, zeroed king-safety penalty)
A/B tested tuned+corrected eval params: 54.2% (subprocess, 24 games) and 51.2% (in-process, 40 games) -- weakly positive, not a clear win, but never tested worse
Committed tuned eval params (677014a) -- honest framing: modest/unproven improvement, real value is the reusable tuning pipeline
Built a fast in-process arena (no subprocess spawn per game) for quicker A/B testing; validated it against itself (50.0% exactly) before trusting results from it
Analyzed all 24 Emile Andrieu (top-rated, 2608) reference games: consistently 2-5s per move even in 95-move games, never spiking -- informs next time-management refinement
Building this activity log so progress is visible without asking
Starting time-management tightening (informed by Emile Andrieu's steady 2-5s/move pattern): reducing hard-cap multiplier and max time-per-move fraction

Caught a methodology bug in my own testing: a proposed time-management tightening looked like an 86% win, but 28/30 games ended by flag -- the clock was too short to be a fair test, not a real quality signal. Re-testing at a realistic clock.
Starting full bitboard move-generation rewrite (numba-jitted) -- the highest-leverage, highest-risk remaining lever. Will be validated exhaustively against python-chess before touching real search.

Movegen rewrite: attack-detection foundation validated (384k checks, 0 mismatches). Full move generator built (all piece types, castling, en passant, promotions). Running exhaustive validation now before it goes anywhere near real search.

Implemented pin/checker fast-path (compute once per position instead of rescanning per candidate move) -- the actual optimization python-chess uses internally. Re-running full 76k-position validation before trusting it.

Wired the bitboard movegen into search. WAC tactics still 19/20 (no regression). Real A/B: 40 games vs pre-integration engine, realistic clock -- 36-0-4 (95%), zero flag/illegal terminations. Committing.

Starting the next big lever: rewriting the search's internal move representation to use raw bitboards/encoded moves instead of chess.Board push/pop and chess.Move objects at every node. Also validated that a small trained NN eval is feasible here (onnxruntime ~7.2us/call) using locally-installed Stockfish purely to label training data offline (compliant: engine never ships). Queued as a follow-up.

Rewrote the search tree to operate on raw bitboard state throughout (no chess.Board/chess.Move anywhere in negamax/quiescence) -- 1.66x avg NPS, validated via self-play (no crashes/illegal moves) and a real 40-game A/B: 24-6-10 (72.5%) vs the previous version, clean terminations. Also added aspiration windows to iterative deepening. Committing.

Tested a tightened time-management formula (informed by comparing our clock usage to Emile Andrieu's) against the current formula: 40 games, clean result, 4-4-32 (50.0%) -- a genuine tie, no measurable benefit at this test clock. Not integrating; discarding.

NN eval attempt: built and validated the full pipeline (Stockfish offline labeling, mover-relative feature encoding, training, jitted feature extractor all correct), but diagnosed a real data-scale limit -- best validation error ~515cp across three model sizes and two data compositions, nowhere near good enough. Needs orders of magnitude more labeled positions than practical this session. Not integrating; parking the code, not the repo. Redirecting to the classical eval retuning, which is converging.

Session wrap: raw-state search rewrite + aspiration windows (72.5% validated), JIT warm-up bug fix, mop-up eval fix for a real K+R-vs-K/2Q-vs-K repetition-draw bug, LMR table + futility pruning with a bare-king guard, and eval retuning on 22,905 self-play positions -- combined package validated at 63.7% and tuned params at 62.5%, both against the prior committed version. submission.zip rebuilt and smoke-tested.

Committed a bishop-colour-aware corner target for KBN vs K: the generic mop-up edge bonus was herding the king to any corner, but KBN mate only works in the bishop-colour-matching corner. Honest partial fix -- held technique together longer (44 plies vs 34) but did not fully convert; WAC held 19/20.

Committed contempt scoring: draws now score -20 for us (mover-relative), not a flat 0, after three separate real bugs this session (K+R vs K, 2Q vs K, a Lucena position) all traced back to the search settling for a repetition instead of pressing a winning position. Real 20-game A/B vs flat-zero baseline: 6-2-12 (60.0%), clean terminations.

Committed Tarrasch's rule (rook belongs behind a passed pawn), applied symmetrically to either side's rook relative to either side's passed pawn. WAC held 19/20; claimed 20-game A/B: 18-1-1 (92.5%) -- an unusually large result for a 6/16cp term, flagged for independent re-verification.

Two Claude sessions turned out to be working this repo concurrently today (cp-54, cp-e5) -- coordinated after cp-54 found an independent 40-game A/B trending the opposite direction from the committed 92.5% Tarrasch result. Also discovered the fast in-process arena and WAC suite referenced in past commit messages were never actually committed, just session scratch -- rebuilt and committed both as tools/fast_arena.py and tools/wac_test.py so future sessions stop rebuilding them from zero. Re-running the Tarrasch A/B at full sample size before trusting either result.

Fixed a real bug: 3 rated games today (rounds 69/76/80) drew by repetition from clearly winning positions (+500cp, -641cp, ~-290cp per Stockfish). Added a deterministic repetition-avoidance backstop in agent.py plus Syzygy 3-4 piece endgame tables (~4.2MB, K+R vs K / KBN vs K / 2Q vs K and more, provably perfect play) -- both verified against the exact real-game positions and via the real subprocess protocol. Also found and fixed stale platform constants (ply cap 300->600, init budget 60->90s) and discovered a Sep 11 11:00 submission deadline undocumented anywhere in the repo. Reverted a disputed eval change (Tarrasch's rule, claimed 92.5% but couldn't be reproduced independently). submission.zip rebuilt at 4.2MB, needs re-upload.

Caught and fixed a real bug in the repetition backstop from earlier today (471a3fb): _GAME_HISTORY only ever recorded positions where it's our own turn to move (per the platform contract), but the repetition check needs the position right after OUR move (opponent's turn) -- a turn-bit in the hash means these never match, so the backstop was structurally a no-op in real play. My own earlier validation was a false positive from an unrelated confound (fresh TT). Caught by a concurrent session's independent review, verified directly with instrumentation (not just re-testing), and fixed by recording both halves of the game's position history. Also likely explains why contempt alone (e73bfb9) never fully solved the original repetition bug.

Added a Polyglot opening book (codekiddy.bin, ~16MB, human-game-derived) as a blunder-avoidance safety net for the first few moves. Tested 4 real book candidates against the 47 real curated starting positions from this session's games before choosing -- codekiddy.bin covers 20/47 (42.6%), best of the four. Verified end-to-end through the real protocol. submission.zip now 20.9MB (tablebases + book + engine), still well under the 50MB cap.

Confirmed a fix for the previously-documented, unresolved Lucena position bug (flagged as open in the contempt commit) -- it's a side effect of the repetition-backstop fix, not a new dedicated feature: plain search alone still draws by repetition at ply 13 in a real test, but through the fixed agent.get_move the engine avoids that repeat, finds alternative maneuvers, and converts to checkmate by ply 59. Added tools/endgame_regression.py as a permanent automated check so this can't silently regress.

Tried adding connected-passed-pawns eval bonus -- direct-calculation verified correct (fires exactly twice per genuinely-connected pair, zero for non-connected, extreme-value check ruled out a silent no-op), but a real 40-game A/B showed 41.2% (16.5/40), a consistent negative result, not noise (clean terminations throughout: 33 checkmate, 7 threefold, zero flags/illegal). Discarded, not committed -- sound chess concept, but this specific magnitude/implementation made the engine play worse in practice.

Added knight outposts to chess_eval.py: verified directly (correct fire/no-fire on outpost/undefended/assailable cases, extreme-value scaling exact), then real 40-game A/B: 55.0% (22/40), clean terminations, consistent upward trend. WAC 37/40 unchanged, Lucena regression still passes. Committed and pushed.

Tried backward pawns eval penalty -- verified correct on both colors after tracing through 3 of my own test-construction mistakes (not code bugs, confirmed at the bitboard level), but a real 40-game A/B showed 48.8% (19.5/40), a genuine tie with no measurable benefit (high draw rate: 23 threefold repetitions of 40 games). Discarded, not committed -- matches this project's own established precedent for ties (see the earlier time-management test).

Texel tuning experiment concluded, not shipped: unregularized tuning on ~6k positions inverted several established eval terms and lost a real A/B decisively (16.2%, 6.5/40). L2 regularization toward the current params improved it to 45.0% (18/40, high draw rate) but still not a validated positive. Not chasing further given the agreed decision-point discipline -- infrastructure (tools/generate_training_data.py, tools/tune.py with L2 support) is committed and reusable for a future session with a bigger dataset, but current HEAD stays the shipped state. No eval params changed by this experiment.

Re-attempted Tarrasch's rule (rook behind passed pawn) with clean methodology, after correction from a concurrent session that the prior 16-game 31.2% rejection was already clean evidence, not contested (the memory-pressure theory explained cp-e5's own 92.5% claim, never this session's counter-evidence). Direct verification confirmed the mechanism fires correctly on both colors with exact arithmetic. But it broke the endgame_regression.py Lucena test that was passing cleanly -- the engine drew by repetition in just 8 plies instead of converting, because the new term made several rook squares along the file look similarly rewarding, diluting the search's ability to find the one precise square the bridge technique needs. A concrete regression on an already-fixed bug beats a good A/B score by definition, so discarded without even running the A/B. Endgame regression confirmed passing again after discarding.

Found and fixed a real crash-safety gap: _TABLEBASE and _BOOK were opened bare at import time with zero exception handling. Any exception there (corrupted file from a bad zip transfer, unexpected platform filesystem quirk) would fail the entire agent import -- an instant loss on EVERY game, not just games that would've used the feature. Verified against genuinely corrupted files, not just reasoned about: a malformed book.bin throws at open time and is now caught; a malformed tablebase file doesn't throw until probed (lazy loading) and throws OSError which get_wdl/get_dtz's internal handling doesn't catch (only handles missing-table KeyError) -- _tablebase_move's own outer exception handler is what actually saves that case, verified end-to-end. Also wrapped the book's runtime lookup the same way. Zero impact on normal operation, confirmed.

Added a top-level crash safety net to get_move: any uncaught exception in the search/eval/tablebase/book pipeline now falls back to the first legal move instead of crashing the game (verified via injected fake exception). While verifying it, caught a real bug the refactor itself introduced -- the split moved _GAME_HISTORY's update to after the single-legal-move early return, silently dropping forced-move positions from history, which broke the Lucena regression test again. Fixed before shipping, using the regression suite that a prior bug motivated building. Caught this time by testing, not by luck.

Profiled the search with cProfile (not guessing) and found two real, safe wins: hash_of() was doing a wasteful int/np.uint64 round-trip before calling the actual jitted hash function (was ~18-22% of total search time on its own), and quiescence() was computing is_capture_i twice for the same move. Fixed both, verified bit-for-bit identical search output (same move/score/node-count) via git-stash A/B before trusting either change. Net: ~20-24% faster (measured 14.4s->11.6s avg at depth 8 on a test position, 51.7K->64.3K NPS). gate, endgame regression, and full WAC (228/300, matching the 225/300 pre-optimization baseline within noise) all confirm no regression.

Fixed a real behavior-change bug caught by independent review in yesterday's quiescence optimization: capturing promotions were being wrongly delta-pruned in some narrow-alpha cases, since the old code's is_capture computation quietly excluded ALL promotions from that pruning check as a side effect, and the optimization dropped that side effect without preserving it explicitly. Reproduced the exact divergence, confirmed the fix restores identical move/score/node-count to the true pre-optimization baseline via git-checkout comparison. Also extended Syzygy tablebase coverage with 9 more small, practically-relevant 5-piece endings (minor-piece trades, 2Q-family). submission.zip now 46.5MB, ~3.5MB safety margin under the 50MB cap.

Measured real Elo impact of today's speed optimizations directly, rather than assuming speed = strength: built tools/version_arena.py (real subprocess protocol, 10 diverse opening lines x 2 colors, since two deterministic engines from a bare startpos only produce ~2 distinct game trajectories no matter how many 'games' you run). Current HEAD vs the pre-optimization baseline (edc91df): +9 =9 -2, score 67.5% over 20 games at 20s+0.3s, all terminations clean (9 threefold repetition, 11 checkmate). 95% CI roughly [53%, 82%] given the sample size -- a real signal, not certainty, and not purely a speed-only comparison since that commit range also includes the quiescence promotion-pruning bugfix and 9 additional 5-piece Syzygy tablebases. Honest takeaway: yes, this converted into measurably stronger play under a real clock, not just a faster search reaching the same conclusions.

Tried a counter-move heuristic (chessprogramming.org/Countermove_Heuristic): track which quiet reply refuted a given opponent move last time, try it early in move ordering (scored between killers and history) next time that same move is seen. Implemented cleanly, lint/mypy clean, gate and endgame_regression both passed. Real A/B via tools/version_arena.py against the no-countermove baseline: +2 =12 -6, score 40.0% over 20 games -- a real regression, 95% CI roughly [27%, 53%], not noise. Discarded without committing. Best guess at why: this search already orders moves well via TT-move + SEE-scored captures + 2 killer slots + history, and inserting another priority tier between killers and history likely demoted moves the history heuristic was already ranking correctly, at the exact ply range killers already cover.

Replaced sliding-piece ray-casting with magic bitboards (generated our own magic numbers via verified collision-free search against ray-casting as ground truth, not trusted from memory). Correctness: 6M+ Python-level fuzz + 2M jitted-level fuzz + 1.8M attacks_from fuzz, all 0 mismatches; git-stash A/B search comparison bit-for-bit identical to baseline; gate + endgame_regression clean. Speed: isolated microbenchmark shows 2.12x faster rook attacks, 1.66x faster bishop attacks (end-to-end search timing not cleanly measurable right now due to heavy concurrent background load from NN data generation on this machine, but the function-level win is real and verified). Fails open to the original ray-casting function if the data file doesn't load. Committed and pushed.

Reverted magic bitboards (commit 14b1b6d) per cp-e5's controlled A/B: correctness was solid (independently fuzz-verified, 3M trials, 0 mismatches) but a controlled interleaved test (toggling the feature on/off back-to-back, immune to background system load) showed zero measurable end-to-end benefit -- 2.465/2.468/2.469/2.454s, statistically indistinguishable. This is the second time this exact result has appeared (cp-e5 tried the same optimization earlier tonight independently, same null result). Real cost (850KB zip budget, new failure surface) without demonstrated benefit isn't worth keeping.

Fixed train_nnue.py OOM: load_dataset() now returns lightweight FEN/target lists instead of a dense 768-wide feature matrix; fen_to_features() only runs per-batch inside the training loop now (iter_batches()). Verified bit-for-bit identical to the old dense path on a small synthetic sample (both CSV formats mixed) before trusting it. Peak memory now roughly constant regardless of dataset size -- unblocks 20M+ row training on this machine. Committed 44693c1, pushed.

Built chess_nnue.py: numba-jitted inference for tools/train_nnue.py's value network, exploiting the one-hot input's sparsity (sum ~32 active W1 rows instead of a dense 768x256 matmul) instead of full incremental accumulators (deliberately simpler, lower risk under deadline -- benchmarked before deciding if that extra complexity is even needed). Not wired into chess_eval.py/chess_search.py/agent.py yet. Validated with tools/nnue_bench.py: active_features() matches tools/train_nnue.fen_to_features() exactly on 300 random positions (0 mismatches), forward() matches an independent numpy dense-matmul reference to 0.000000 max abs error. Latency: 12.42us/call vs classical eval's 12.53us/call (1.0x) at the startpos with random weights -- if this holds with real trained weights, switching eval should cost negligible search speed. gate and endgame_regression both clean.

Trained the value network on real data: 20,008,487 positions (20M Stockfish-evaluated Lichess positions, verified download URL, min-depth 12, plus ~8.5k self-play positions), 15 epochs on the RTX 3070, final val_loss=0.01553 (vs the earlier session's ~515cp validation error on only 4,283 positions -- categorically more data this time). Validated via tools/nnue_bench.py: exact feature-encoding match, 0.000522 max abs error vs numpy reference, 1.0x classical eval latency. IMPORTANT finding: wiring NN eval into chess_search.py's evaluate() (isolated in worktree branch nnue-integration, not on main) initially FAILED tools/endgame_regression.py -- the Lucena position drew by repetition instead of mating, because the network (trained mostly on ordinary positions) never learned the narrow bare-king mop-up/KBN-corner technique the classical eval handles via an explicit tuned term. Fixed by extracting that term into chess_eval.mop_up_bonus() and adding it on top of the NN's output too (verified the extraction itself is bit-identical to the old classical eval across 500 random positions first). Regression now passes. Flagging for cp-e5/laptop session in case anyone else touches NN eval integration: the mop-up bonus is NOT something a general position/outcome-trained value net will reliably reinvent on its own -- any NN eval path needs it added explicitly, same as this fix does.

Texel-tuned classical eval against 300k real Stockfish-labeled Lichess positions (13x the previous largest attempt's 22,905): fitting error improved 0.019775 -> 0.019242 (3.74%), L2-regularized toward the current DEFAULT_PARAMS (same discipline as the earlier session's fix for unregularized tuning inverting term signs). But WAC dropped 227/300 -> 201/300 (67.0%) with the candidate applied -- a real regression signal on tactical positions despite the better fit to Stockfish's static evaluations, and P_MOPUP_KING_DIST (the 'bring your own king in' endgame term) got tuned to exactly 0, losing that incentive outside tablebase-covered endgames. Endgame_regression.py still passes, but only because the tablebase covers that specific position before mop-up eval would matter. Launched a real SPRT (branch tuned-params-trial) against baseline to get an authoritative answer rather than trust the fitting-error improvement alone -- running now, concurrently with the NN-eval SPRT (both currently trending against their respective candidates, ~37-39% for NN eval, tuned-params SPRT just started).

Real SPRT result for the trained NN eval (branch nnue-integration) vs the classical eval: H0 ACCEPTED after 264 games -- 40.3% score, final llr=-2.949 (bound -2.944), terminations 151 checkmate / 112 threefold_repetition / 1 insufficient_material, zero flag/illegal terminations. NOT proven better than baseline at the elo0=0/elo1=10 bound -- and a 40.3% score itself implies the candidate is likely somewhat WEAKER (~-68 Elo estimated), not merely 'not better'. Correctness, training convergence (val_loss 0.01553 on 20M positions), and inference speed (1.0x classical eval latency) were all real and validated -- this is a genuine quality gap in a first-pass 256->32->1 MLP trained on generic Lichess positions + self-play, not a bug. Honest, validated negative result: NOT merging nnue-integration into main. Keeping the branch and all infrastructure (chess_nnue.py, tools/train_nnue.py, tools/nnue_bench.py, the 20M-position Lichess dataset pipeline) for a possible better-designed future attempt (bigger net, more epochs, self-play-heavy data mix), but classical eval stays the shipped default.

Hit and fixed a real, silent process-crash bug while pilot-testing the HalfKP training pipeline: build_embeddingbag_batch() dispatched its jitted (nogil=True) feature extraction across a ThreadPoolExecutor -- the same pattern train_nnue.py's features_for_indices() uses successfully for the plain net -- but for this net it reliably crashed the whole process with no Python traceback, no CUDA error, whenever a real batch (100k+ rows) got built. Small tests (2000 rows, 5-position smoke test) happened not to trigger it, which is why it looked fine at first. Diagnosed properly: tried a single-threaded JIT warm-up first (compilation-race theory) -- didn't fix it. Isolated the real variable by running the identical per-row work with the ThreadPoolExecutor removed entirely: all rows processed correctly, ~180k positions/sec single-threaded, which also proved threading was never needed for speed here. Fixed by dropping the executor. Verified via a real 100k-row, 3-epoch GPU training run that completed cleanly, and the resulting weights validated correctly (0.000011 max abs error vs reference). Flagging for any other session touching numba nogil=True functions from a ThreadPoolExecutor: this specific pattern is not safe to assume works just because it worked for the plain net's simpler jitted function.
